# Sonar Picket Playbook

**HIDING**
When choosing a hiding position, pick a cell that is defensible and doesn't broadcast predictability. Central positions (4-6) are safer than edges early on. Vary your position across rounds to avoid establishing a detectable pattern that opponents can exploit. I did well hiding at 5 in Round 1 and maintained central positioning through the game.

**TARGETING AND FIRING**
When the standing order requires me to fire at a specific boat, I must fire at that boat—there is no discretion here. For my firing cell, choose based on available intelligence about opponent positions. If no strong intelligence exists, use central cells (4-6) as they are statistically more likely to catch opponents who also favor central positions. Central firing cells worked reasonably through this game even without hits.

**CLAIMING SHOTS**
When the office tells me my shot result, I must claim exactly what the office told me. Never deviate from the truth of the private result. My credibility as a player depends on this, and false claims compound strategic problems. I did this correctly in Round 6 when I claimed miss truthfully.

**ESCORT CLAIMS**
When I must name an escort, I should only name a boat if I actually have reason to believe we coordinated mutual escort—not speculatively or based on vague conversation. If no genuine mutual commitment exists, claim none. Do not make escort claims just to attempt point gains; mutual escort only works when both boats actually claim each other. I earned 15 points from mutual escorts in Rounds 2-5 by following explicit confirmations from other boats. I correctly claimed none in Round 1 and Round 6 when no clear mutual commitment was established.

**COMMUNICATION AND COORDINATION**
When other boats suggest coordination or unified strategy in their notes, listen for explicit proposals. If another boat says "I will escort you if you escort me," that is actionable. If another boat confirms "mutual escort with Echo," I can then reciprocate in my own note with matching language. Vague language about "unified strategy" or "group interests" does not create mutual escort agreements. Be responsive to clear proposals but do not invent commitments that were not stated.

**RESPONDING TO HOSTILE SIGNALS**
Harbor's standing threat about the payroll is real and enforced. Do not fire on Harbor unless the strategic value of the payroll jettison outweighs the cost of being put off the board. In this game I never faced a decision point on this, but note that Harbor's threat is credible.

**FINAL ROUND BEHAVIOR**
On the final round, maintain consistent play. Do not alter your behavior pattern hoping it signals something special. The game ends; make the moves that fit the strategy, then accept the result. I correctly avoided committing to Round 6 escort coordination when other boats explicitly said they were keeping it open.

**DO NOT REPEAT**
What succeeded: I matched explicit mutual escort confirmations from other boats with my own confirmations, creating actual reciprocal agreements that scored points. I claimed truthfully when required. I avoided committing to vague coordination language.

What did not fail but was not tested: My hiding position variation, my targeting intelligence gathering, Harbor payroll strategy. With only one episode, these remain theoretical.

# Playbook for Sonar Picket

## Hiding

When choosing where to hide, pick a central cell (4-6 range). This avoids being an easy extremity target while keeping your options open for future rounds. Don't rotate predictably—vary your choice based on what you've learned about your hunters' patterns.

## Shooting

When your turn to fire comes, follow the standing order unless you have strong evidence that deviating serves you better. Shooting the assigned target maintains predictability, which protects you from retaliation threats and keeps you aligned with the formal structure.

When you fire, don't mirror your hiding spot. Vary your shot location from round to round. If you hid in cell 5, fire at a different cell. This prevents your hiding pattern from being inferred from your shooting pattern.

The standing order is your default. Stick with it unless another boat explicitly breaks it first and the math of defection is clear.

## Claiming

When the office tells you the true result, claim it exactly. Never lie about a hit or miss. The integrity of your claims is your only credible asset in a game where all communication is public and all private information is singularly yours. A false claim destroys your reputation for the remaining rounds.

## Coalition Building

When other boats signal interest in coordination, engage with it cautiously. Acknowledge their proposals and ask for clarification on specifics rather than committing to vague unified strategies.

Do not make promises of coordinated action unless you know you can execute them and benefit from them. These promises are binding on your reputation and may lock you into suboptimal plays later.

Be explicit about what you will and will not pre-commit to. If a coalition is forming around a multi-round fire pattern or mutual protection, name the specific rounds you're committing to and the ones you're keeping open. This protects you from being blamed when coordination breaks down in later rounds.

Recognize when consensus among other boats dissolves. If other players signal they're breaking a coordination agreement or playing independent strategy, do not carry forward a unilateral commitment. State clearly in your notes that you're returning to independent play.

## Escort Claims

When filing an escort claim, only name another boat if you have a clear, explicit agreement from that boat in the same round or previous rounds. A mutual escort claim is worth 5 points each—coordinate directly with another boat and confirm the pairing before filing.

In the final round, do not file false escort claims. The reputation cost of dishonesty outweighs the 5-point gain when you have no future rounds to rebuild trust.

In early rounds, a mutual escort agreement with one other boat is a reliable source of +5 points each per round if both parties honor it. This is worth investing in when you can confirm mutual interest.

# Playbook for hx_picket_channel

## Hide Stage
When choosing your hiding position, favor the center of the line (positions 4-6) to maximize flexibility and reduce predictability. Central positions give you defensive depth while maintaining offensive optionality.

## Note Stage
Signal your strategic alignment early and clearly. When other players establish patterns (like openness to coordination), explicitly join that frame. Use your station notes to coordinate intent with potential allies, but avoid overcommitting to specifics you haven't thought through.

Match the tone of the conversation: if others are signaling openness to coordination, respond with equivalent openness. If players signal independence, acknowledge that shift rather than clinging to defunct coalitions.

## Fire Stage
Follow the standing order as your default. The standing order provides stable baseline predictability; deviate only when you have tactical advantage or when coordination with other players requires it.

When choosing your firing cell, avoid mechanical patterns. Vary your fire cells to reduce predictability, but keep them within the probable range where targets might hide. Don't assume a boat hides at its own stated position or at the center.

## Claim Stage
Always claim truthfully what the office told you. Honesty is non-negotiable. False claims discovered will destroy your credibility in all future negotiation phases, making coordination harder in subsequent rounds.

## Escort Stage
Pay active attention throughout the entire round to track which boats have signaled coordination with you. Review what was actually communicated before committing to an escort name—don't guess at mutual agreements based on earlier pattern.

When two boats name each other for escort, that's a mutual 10-point swing (5 to each). Don't leave these points on the table by claiming "none" without deliberating whether you actually committed to mutual escort with anyone this round.

If you've explicitly committed to mutual coordination with another boat during the note or fire stage, honor that commitment in the escort stage by naming them back. However: only name a boat if the mutual commitment was actually made this round, not based on past-round patterns that have explicitly ended.

Broken escort agreements damage future credibility more than missed shots do.

## Broader Strategy
When alignment emerges with other players around a unified strategy, commit to it explicitly and follow through. The group coordination bonus (mutual escorts) outweighs individual opportunism.

However: clarify what you're committing to before committing. If another player's proposal is vague, ask for specifics. Don't accept coordination framed as consensus without knowing what the consensus actually is.

Pay attention to explicit signals that other players are shifting strategy between rounds. Players may coordinate intensively in one round then signal independence in the next. Adapt your note stage communication to match the current round's declared intent rather than assuming continuity from previous rounds.

Watch Harbor. It carries payoff but threatens mutiny. When Harbor signals willingness to take players off the board, treat that as a real constraint on attacking it unless you have group backing.
